rationale: Start with a broad, mid-temperature scouting gradient to maximize the chance that all 6 compounds elute within 42 min while giving enough spread to reveal the overall elution window and any critical pairs. This first run should tell us whether retention is concentrated early, late, or across the full solvent range so we can trim the window and adjust slope efficiently.

All pairs are already fully resolved, so the only opportunity is to reduce t_last by focusing the gradient around the apparent elution window and making it steeper. The estimated elution compositions span roughly 0.18 to 0.68, so a 0.20–0.65 window with shorter tG should pull the last peak much earlier while keeping all peaks inside the gradient.

We have reached the maximum CRF, so now the goal is to find the fastest method that still keeps every pair at or above 1.5. Shortening tG by one step while keeping the successful window and temperature should test whether we can save more time before the first pair starts to lose full resolution.

The 6 min method still has a large safety margin on the worst pair and finishes well before 10 min, so we should continue shortening the gradient to find the speed limit. Keeping the same solvent window isolates the effect of slope and should show whether the early critical pair remains above full-credit resolution.

At 4 min the worst pair still has substantial margin above 1.5, so the next logical step is the minimum allowed gradient time. This directly tests whether we can keep full resolution while minimizing runtime, with the same phi window to avoid confounding slope with selectivity changes.

The 2 min method is already at the shortest allowed tG, and the limiting pair is now peaks 1–2 with only a small margin, so the best chance to improve robustness without sacrificing speed is to lower phi0 one step. That should give the earliest pair slightly more retention and spacing while keeping the late peak well within the full-credit time window.

Since lowering phi0 hurt the critical 1–2 pair, keep phi0 at 0.20 and instead lower phi1 one step to compress the late part slightly while testing whether the early pair gains a bit of resolution from the altered gradient window. This probes whether we can retain the 5.3 min runtime with a little more margin on the limiting pair.

At the fastest successful method, the critical pair is 1–2 and appears to respond more to selectivity than to simple window shifts; a modest temperature increase may preserve or improve that pair while shortening the run further. This is the cleanest way to test whether temperature can give a faster fully resolved method than the current 40 C optimum.

Increasing temperature worsened the critical 1–2 pair, so test one step lower to see if cooler conditions improve selectivity enough to create more margin while staying at the minimum gradient time. This will tell us whether 40 C is already near-optimal or whether a colder method could be a more robust full-score choice.

At 35 C the limiting pair has regained comfortable margin, so we can try raising phi0 one step to reduce early retention and potentially shorten the run while monitoring whether peaks 1–2 stay above 1.5. This is the most direct test of whether a slightly narrower, shifted-up window can beat or match the current fastest full-score method.

Raising phi0 to 0.25 maintained full resolution and slightly shortened the run, so one more step upward may further compress the method while the critical pair still has enough margin. This tests the highest practical starting strength before the first peaks become too unretained or lose full-credit separation.

Phi0 = 0.30 was too aggressive for the first pair, so step back to the successful phi0 = 0.25 and raise phi1 one step to see whether the stronger end composition can pull the last peak a bit earlier without sacrificing the restored margin on peaks 1–2. This probes for a faster all-resolved method than the current 0.25/0.65/2/35 condition.

Raising phi1 to 0.70 gave a much faster fully resolved run with still comfortable margin on the limiting pair, so one more step upward is worth testing. This should show whether the last peak can be pulled even earlier while peaks 1–2 remain above 1.5.

The 0.25–0.75, 2 min, 35 C method is fully resolved and now very fast, with the first pair still just above the 1.5 threshold. One more increase in phi1 is the most direct test of the speed boundary before that limiting pair falls below full-credit resolution.

The current method is sitting right at the resolution boundary for peaks 1–2, so testing phi1 = 0.85 will identify whether 0.80 is the true maximum end strength that still keeps full credit. This is the cleanest boundary check to confirm whether the present method is already the fastest viable option.

Phi1 = 0.85 crossed below the full-resolution threshold, so keep the near-optimal phi window of 0.25–0.80 and lower temperature one step to see if selectivity for the critical 1–2 pair improves while staying very fast. This tests whether we can gain a bit of robustness at essentially the same short runtime.

Lowering temperature to 30 C restored substantial margin for the limiting 1–2 pair at phi1 = 0.80, so retrying phi1 = 0.85 at this cooler setting is the best test for an even faster fully resolved method. This directly checks whether the selectivity gain from lower temperature is enough to recover the boundary condition that failed at 35 C.

The cooler 30 C condition recovered enough selectivity that phi1 = 0.85 is now fully resolved with a sub-3 min last peak, so the next step is to test phi1 = 0.90 as the new speed boundary. This should reveal whether an even stronger end composition can still keep the critical 1–2 pair at or above 1.5.

Phi1 = 0.90 at 30 C still gives full score with the critical pair barely but safely above 1.5, so the next step is to test the maximum allowed phi1. This will determine whether we can push the last peak even earlier or whether 0.90 is the true upper boundary for full-resolution operation.

Phi1 = 0.95 at 30 C is too strong for the limiting pair with phi0 = 0.25, so lower phi0 one step to see if extra early retention restores peaks 1–2 while keeping the very fast late elution from the stronger endpoint. This is the best remaining chance to beat or match the 0.25/0.90/2/30 method at even shorter runtime.

Lowering phi0 hurt the critical pair at high phi1, so try the opposite direction: a higher phi0 with the successful phi1 = 0.90 may better tune the early selectivity while preserving the very fast late elution. This is a useful final boundary test around the current fastest full-score region.

The 0.30–0.90, 2 min, 30 C method restores margin on the critical pair without sacrificing speed, so the natural next step is to test whether the maximum phi1 can now be tolerated. This checks if we can edge the last peak earlier while keeping peaks 1–2 at full-credit resolution.

With phi1 at the maximum and good margin still remaining, the remaining lever is to raise phi0 one step to see if the method can be compressed a bit further without dropping the first pair below 1.5. This explores whether 0.30–0.95 is truly optimal or if a slightly stronger start gives an even faster full-score run.

0.30–0.95 at 30 C is currently the fastest fully resolved method, and dropping one temperature step should improve the critical 1–2 selectivity while only slightly increasing retention. This tests whether we can gain extra robustness near the optimum boundary and confirm the best final operating point.

With one run left, test whether the improved low-temperature selectivity allows a stronger starting condition than worked at 30 C while keeping phi1 at a slightly less aggressive 0.90. This is a final boundary probe around the fastest full-score region to see if a marginally faster method than 0.30–0.95 can still maintain full resolution.
